unmatched_peer.body:
`assert False` is stripped when Python is run with `-O` (optimize flag). When that happens, `listen_for_disconnect` receives an unrecognised message type, falls through the `if` block, and returns `None` implicitly. If the disconnect task finishes first, `done.result()` returns `None` and the code falls through to `await self.send_response(None, send)`, which crashes with an `AttributeError` instead of surfacing a useful error. This was called out by @felixxm in the inline review but the fix wasn't applied. Use a real exception:

```python
raise ValueError(
    "Invalid ASGI message after request body: %s" % message["type"]
)
```
unmatched_peer.rationale: @felixxm explicitly requested this change in the PR inline review ('We should raise a proper exception instead of using `assert` e.g. `ValueError`') and it was not addressed. `assert` statements are compiled out under `python -O`, making the guard a no-op in optimised deployments.

unmatched_peer.body:
`asyncio.wait` with `return_when=FIRST_COMPLETED` guarantees *at least* one future in `done`, but both can complete before the event loop yields control (e.g., a very fast view and an already-queued disconnect). When both tasks land in `done`, `pending` is an empty set and `pending.pop()` raises `KeyError`.

A safer pattern:
```python
done_task = done.pop()
pending_tasks = list(pending)
# cancel remaining
for t in pending_tasks:
    t.cancel()
    try:
        await t
    except (asyncio.CancelledError, Exception):
        pass
```
or guard with `if pending:` before calling `.pop()`.
unmatched_peer.rationale: Python's `set.pop()` raises `KeyError` on an empty set. `asyncio.wait` docs state it returns 'a set of Tasks/Futures that are done' and 'a set of Tasks/Futures that are not yet done' — the pending set can be empty if all awaitables finished concurrently.

unmatched_peer.body: `body_file` is only closed in the `RequestAborted` and `AssertionError` branches. Any other exception raised by `done.result()` (e.g., an unhandled exception that escapes Django's middleware/view error handling) or by `await pending` (e.g., a view's cleanup code that raises after catching `CancelledError`) propagates without calling `body_file.close()`, leaking a `SpooledTemporaryFile` that may have spilled to disk. A `try/finally` block that calls `body_file.close()` on all exit paths would be safer.
unmatched_peer.rationale: The `SpooledTemporaryFile` is opened in `read_body` and the caller is responsible for closing it. The two existing `close()` calls cover known-exceptional paths only; unexpected exceptions escape without cleanup.

unmatched_peer.body: `time.sleep(1)` in a synchronous view blocks a thread-pool thread for one full second. Because Django wraps it with `sync_to_async`, the event loop stays responsive, but every test that exercises `/delayed_hello/` will take at least one second. Using `asyncio.sleep` in a proper `async` view (or a much shorter sleep, e.g. 0.1 s) would keep the test suite fast without changing the scenario's semantics.
unmatched_peer.rationale: `test_delayed_disconnect_with_body` routes to this view. The only requirement is that the disconnect arrives while the view is still in progress; a 1-second sleep is far more than needed and makes the test suite noticeably slow.

unmatched_peer.body: The test relies on a fixed 0.1-second sleep to ensure the view (which sleeps 0.2 s) is already in progress before the disconnect is sent. Under heavy CI load the event loop may not schedule the view's `asyncio.sleep(0.2)` before the test's `asyncio.sleep(0.1)` expires, making the timing relationship between the two sleeps non-deterministic. A synchronisation primitive (e.g. an `asyncio.Event` set by the view at startup) would make this race-free.
unmatched_peer.rationale: The view sleeps 0.2 s and the test waits 0.1 s before disconnecting. Both are wall-clock estimates; under load, both `asyncio.sleep` calls fire on the same event loop, so their relative ordering is not strictly guaranteed by the numeric values alone.

unmatched_peer.body: The documentation says "an `asyncio.CancelledError` will be raised *in the view*". This is accurate only for async views. For synchronous views wrapped via `sync_to_async`, the cancellation cancels the wrapping coroutine, not the blocking thread — `CancelledError` is never delivered inside the sync view function. The note should clarify this only applies to `async` views.
unmatched_peer.rationale: The ASGI handler's concurrent task wraps `get_response_async`, which uses `sync_to_async` for sync views. A thread running a sync view cannot receive `asyncio.CancelledError`; the cancellation only surfaces at the `await` boundary in the async wrapper.

unmatched_peer.body: The disconnect-cancellation behaviour described here is ASGI-only, but the section doesn't say so. Developers using WSGI (the default) may read this and incorrectly expect `asyncio.CancelledError` to be raised in their streaming generators.
unmatched_peer.rationale: The `StreamingHttpResponse` class is used under both WSGI and ASGI. The new handler logic that cancels `process_request` on disconnect lives in `ASGIHandler.handle()` (django/core/handlers/asgi.py), so it never fires under WSGI. Without an explicit ASGI qualifier the section is misleading to WSGI users. The existing `async.txt` section already scopes itself to ASGI via its surrounding context; this new sub-section in `request-response.txt` lacks that scope.

unmatched_peer.body: `test_streaming` fetches `http.response.start` but never asserts its `type` or `status`, so a 500 error response would pass this test undetected. All other response-start checks in this file assert both fields (e.g. `test_get_asgi_application`, `test_asyncio_streaming_cancel_error`). Similarly the fourth `receive_output` call at line 503 is unasserted — it should at minimum verify `type == "http.response.body"` and `more_body == False` (the ASGI end-of-stream sentinel).
unmatched_peer.rationale: The pattern in this test class is to assert `response_start['type'] == 'http.response.start'` and `response_start['status'] == 200` immediately after every `http.response.start` receive. This test skips those checks for a new endpoint that has no other coverage.

Unlike the old code where `send_response` ran in the main coroutine (and could also leak, a pre-existing issue), `process_request` now wraps both `run_get_response` *and* `send_response` inside the cancellable task. That means streaming-iterator cleanup code (`finally` / `except CancelledError`) now executes inside the task. If that cleanup raises, the task ends with a non-`CancelledError` exception, `await task` propagates it past the `except asyncio.CancelledError: pass`, and `body_file.close()` is bypassed. The `SpooledTemporaryFile` is then left open until GC, which triggers the `ResourceWarning` on Python 3.12+ noted in the PR discussion.

unmatched_peer.body:
`functools._lru_cache_wrapper` is a private implementation detail (leading underscore). Although it has been stable in CPython since Python 3.2, it is not part of the public API and could be renamed or removed in a future Python release without a deprecation notice. Django's migration serializer hardcoding a private name creates a silent failure mode: if the name changes, the type simply won't be found in the registry and users will get confusing serialization errors.

A safer approach is to derive the type from the public API once at module import time:
```python
_lru_cache_wrapper_type = type(functools.lru_cache(maxsize=None)(lambda: None))
```
and use `_lru_cache_wrapper_type` in the registry tuple.
unmatched_peer.rationale: The name `functools._lru_cache_wrapper` is explicitly private (leading underscore). Django already takes pains elsewhere to avoid relying on private CPython internals. Using a computed type avoids the coupling without any functional difference.

unmatched_peer.body: `test_serialize_decorated_functions` relies solely on `assertSerializedEqual` (round-trip), but never asserts the exact serialized string. This means a regression where `function_with_cache` serialized to something like `'functools.lru_cache.<locals>.wrapper'` instead of `'tests.migrations.test_writer.function_with_cache'` would go undetected as long as the import happens to succeed. Asserting `assertSerializedResultEqual(function_with_cache, ("tests.migrations.test_writer.function_with_cache", {"import tests.migrations.test_writer"}))` (or equivalent) would pin the expected output and make the intent explicit.
unmatched_peer.rationale: The adjacent `test_serialize_functions` test calls `serialize_round_trip` and checks exact strings (e.g. `"models.SET(42)"`). The new test lacks the same level of assertion, so it cannot detect a case where the wrapper's qualified name rather than the original function's name is emitted.

unmatched_peer.body: The sub-bullet says functions "may be decorated if wrapped properly, i.e. using `functools.wraps`". Using `functools.wraps` is the canonical way, but what the serializer actually requires is that `__module__` and `__qualname__` are set correctly on the wrapper. "i.e." implies it is the *only* way; "e.g." (for example) would be more accurate and leave room for other valid approaches.
unmatched_peer.rationale: `FunctionTypeSerializer` depends on `__module__` and `__qualname__` being present on the object, not specifically on `functools.wraps`. Any decorator that copies those attributes would work; using "i.e." instead of "e.g." overstates the constraint.

unmatched_peer.body:
When `error_messages=None`, `self.error_messages` is assigned the same dict object as `Paginator.default_error_messages` (the class-level attribute), not a copy. Any code that mutates the instance's `error_messages` dict (e.g. `paginator.error_messages["invalid_page"] = "oops"`) will corrupt the class-level default, affecting every subsequently created `Paginator` instance that also omits `error_messages`.

Always produce a new dict by applying `|` unconditionally:
```python
self.error_messages = self.default_error_messages | (error_messages or {})
```
This is a one-liner, removes the conditional branch, and always gives each instance its own dict.
unmatched_peer.rationale: The `if error_messages is None` branch on line 51-52 evaluates to `self.default_error_messages` and assigns that exact object to the instance attribute. Python dict `|` always returns a new dict, so the `else` branch is safe, but the `None` branch is not.
